title: What Is Inflation?
paragraphs: If you compare prices today with prices a few years ago, you will probably notice that most things have become more expensive. This general rise in prices over time is called inflation, and it is one of the most closely watched numbers in any economy.

Inflation reduces what money can buy. A salary that stays the same while prices rise is worth less in real terms. Statistics offices measure inflation with a consumer price index: they track the cost of a typical basket of goods and services, such as food, housing and transport, and calculate how much it changes over twelve months.

There are several causes. Demand-pull inflation happens when people and businesses want to buy more than the economy can produce. Cost-push inflation happens when production becomes more expensive, for example because of higher energy prices, and companies pass these costs on to customers.

Central banks are responsible for keeping inflation under control, and many of them aim for a rate of around two percent a year. Their main tool is the interest rate: by raising it, they make loans more expensive, which slows spending and, over time, helps prices rise more slowly.
